articles.body: Let me get this straight: Because President Trump launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran for the purpose of denying the mullahs access to a nuclear weapon — a red line that every U.S. politician has embraced in the past — and because Americans are paying more for gasoline and diesel than they were a year ago, voters are now set to elect anti-U.S., anti-Israel candidates who want to destroy the economic system and institutions that have made the United States the strongest, most prosperous nation on earth. Did I get that wrong? Has Americans’ hatred of Donald Trump made them simple? Do they really think that Democrats like Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for a vacant Senate seat in Michigan, loves our country and aligns with our values? The candidate who, when pressed, would not explicitly condemn Iran’s Revolutionary Guard — the thugs who killed tens of thousands of their own countrymen and have orchestrated the murders of thousands of Americans through their villainous terror proxies? El-Sayed, who spouted the wonders of Medicare for All and promised to eliminate private insurance until it threatened to derail his campaign, flip-flopping on a central plank in his platform? El-Sayed, who calls Hasan Piker, the anti-American Israel-hater who said "Americans deserved 9/11" a friend? Come on, folks, that’s not who we are. MORNING GLORY: ROGERS VERSUS EL-SAYED IS A REFERENDUM ON THE FUTURE OF AMERICA Here are three reasons why voters must come to their senses before they commit a grievous error in the midterms: 1. Democrats promise "affordability," but always deliver higher prices. Always. 2. Voters need to look at our economy — not the alarmist headlines crowning liberal publications, but the growth that is happening under our feet, and understand that Democrats will reverse our progress. 3. Americans also must realize how quickly Democrats will revert to the policies that voters turned against two years ago: an open border that allowed millions of unvetted people to enter our country illegally, soft-on-crime regulations that handicapped our cops and made our streets more dangerous, and green energy diktats that strangled America’s abundant fossil fuels industry, eliminating a gigantic competitive advantage. Do we really want to go back to Joe Biden’s woke and feckless America? There were good reasons that Americans elected Donald Trump in 2024; those reasons still exist. OUR CLOSING ARGUMENT: THE MIDTERMS ARE A REFERENDUM ON WHO RUNS YOUR LIFE Let’s start with the absurd notion that Democrats can deliver "affordability." Of the ten most expensive states in the U.S., all but Alaska are run by Democrats. Of the top ten most expensive cities in the U.S., all but Miami are run by Democrats. Is this a coincidence? No. Democrats favor high taxes and cumbersome regulations; both drive costs higher as businesses pass those charges along to their customers. California imposes a 74 cent per gallon tax on gasoline — the country’s highest. New York’s horrendously complex building regulations mean it takes longer to build in New York than any other place on earth (literally), which drives housing costs higher. Governor Kathy Hochul slapped a recurring $22 Congestion Pricing fee on big trucks delivering groceries or other goods to New York City stores — who do you think pays for that? THE DSA’S DANGEROUS FINE PRINT. THEY'RE COMING FOR MILLIONAIRES (AND YOU) Democrats like to spend, and they like to tax. When she ran for president in 2024, Kamala Harris wanted to roll back Trump’s 2017 tax cuts that put $2,000 extra cash in the pockets of the average American family; every single Democrat in Congress voted against the Big, Beautiful Bill that cut taxes on tips and overtime and delivered thousands of dollars more for working people. Joe Biden increased the federal government workforce to a record high of around 3 million (excluding Census years); Donald Trump has shrunk that body to 2.67 million. Trump thinks it’s more important to grow manufacturing jobs than the federal bureaucracy. That’s what’s happening now. DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT Democrats want to expand welfare programs, doling out taxpayer-funded benefits even to people not in the country legally; Republicans want to cut back on spending, in part by rooting out fraud and waste. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Because President Trump’s team has rolled back regulations and cut taxes, business is booming. The economy is growing at better than 5%, according to the Atlanta Fed, with investment soaring, especially in AI-related businesses. Americans have been led (in part by Chinese propaganda) to fear AI, but as this dazzling new technology delivers new cures for cancer, improvements in our failing education system (which Democrat-supporting teachers unions will oppose) and boosts business productivity, the country will prosper. Yes, the government should work with the AI companies to ensure our safety. No, Congress should not be given any role in the oversight. Trump has this right. Child poverty in the U.S. dropped to an all-time low last year, while real median household income was the highest on record. Household net worth is up 17% since Donald Trump took office in January 2025 and the stock market is hovering near all-time highs, benefiting the 62% of Americans who own stocks directly or indirectly. All these wins could evaporate if Democrats take power. MORNING GLORY: FIVE SENATE RACES SHOW WHY DEMOCRATS MAY REGRET THEIR PRIMARY CHOICES How would that happen? First, Democrats will reopen the border; some candidates like House contender Darialisa Avila Chevalier want to eliminate it altogether. Second, the party, led by non-Democrat Bernie Sanders, will move to hamstring the growth of AI, benefiting only China. Third, a Democratic Congress will loosen recent changes to Medicaid eligibility; our welfare ranks and spending will start to grow again. Fourth, as Joe Biden did, they will try to slow down the growth of U.S. oil and natural gas production by again taking Alaskan acreage out of play, reining in LNG exports or cutting back lease sales and drilling permits. Fifth, they will fight any extension of Trump’s tax cuts, increasing uncertainty and dampening business investment. articles.title: Pokimane explains how her cat Mimi died after balcony fall and addresses online criticism
articles.summary: Twitch streamer Pokimane has shared details about the heartbreaking death of her cat Mimi, who died after falling from a balcony.
articles.body: Twitch streamer Pokimane has shared details about the heartbreaking death of her cat Mimi, who died after falling from a balcony. The streamer said the accident happened after cleaners opened her balcony door and left its screen door open. Mimi had been part of her life for eight years, making the loss deeply painful. After sharing the news, Pokimane faced questions and criticism online, prompting her to explain what happened. She also made it clear that she did not want to blame anyone for the tragic accident.Pokimane reveals how Mimi’s balcony fall led to her tragic deathPokimane explained that she had always taken steps to keep her cats safe on balconies. In a post on X, she said she had used bird spikes and plastic covers to protect every balcony in her previous homes. However, the building she currently lives in did not allow her to install these safety measures.She also explained that her balcony door had a bug screen to stop insects from entering her home. According to Pokimane, the cleaners opened the balcony door to let fresh air inside, not to clean the balcony. She said she had never asked them to clean that area.Pokimane added that the cleaners did not close the screen door after opening it. A few minutes later, Mimi stepped out onto the balcony and fell.The streamer said she learned that Mimi had been taken to an emergency room while she was live-streaming Valorant on September 28. She quickly ended the broadcast and rushed to the vet. Sadly, the doctor told her that Mimi had not survived.Pokimane later returned to her stream and became emotional while speaking about her cat. She said, “I can't believe my baby is gone,” and described Mimi as her beloved pet.Pokimane addresses online criticism and calls it a freak accidentAfter sharing the news, Pokimane posted another message on X to explain the circumstances of Mimi’s death. She said she should not have to clarify details while grieving, but decided to speak out because some people online were making negative comments.Pokimane explained that she had taken safety steps in her previous homes and that the current building’s rules had prevented her from using the same balcony protections. She also clarified that the cleaners had opened the door to let in a breeze, rather than to clean the balcony.Despite the painful loss, Pokimane said she did not want to blame anyone. She described the incident as a “heartbreaking, freak accident” and said she was very sad.In her original post, she had also apologized for suddenly leaving her livestream, explaining that she had been told Mimi was in the emergency room. She ended the message with the words, “I love you forever, Mimi.”Mimi had been with Pokimane for eight years, and viewers had seen the cat throughout much of the streamer’s online journey. Her death has left Pokimane heartbroken. While she has clarified how the accident happened, she has asked for understanding as she deals with the loss of her beloved pet.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the early 1970s, a South Carolina contractor began casting famous buildings in his backyard; by 1998, his 33-piece Concrete City had been rescued by a state museum
articles.summary: Explore the remarkable story of L.C. Carson, a South Carolina contractor who created Concrete City in his backyard—a collection of 33 architectural replicas that now inspires future generations in a state museum. Discover the preservation efforts and the impact of self-taught creators on cultural heritage.
articles.body: Every builder has a project of their dreams. Some see it as a church, while others see it as a bridge or a large public space. Many people spend their entire careers building on other people's ideas, without ever having the chance to create something truly original. One contractor in Orangeburg County, South Carolina, chose to begin construction in his yard without waiting for a commission.Leslie Cosgrove Carson, or L.C., was his name. He dropped out of school to support his family during the Great Depression and worked as a contractor for 47 years, according to the South Carolina State Museum. He started creating scale replicas of well-known buildings in the early 1970s, and the project developed into Concrete City, a collection of 33 waist-high skyscrapers that the museum eventually took in and preserved.From the job sites to a back gardenCarson was self-schooled in history, mythology and art history and journeyed to Europe and Central America to see some of the sites he had only read about firsthand. Back home he applied what he knew best. The museum says he built his copies of the Parthenon, the Sphinx, Rameses’ Temple and the Colosseum from ordinary building materials, and the finished pieces represented the techniques of a working builder.A colourful profile of Roger Manley’s book Weird Carolinas appears in the Times and Democrat of Orangeburg. Carson got the idea after he visited the Ave Maria Grotto in Cullman, Ala., and decided to copy buildings from throughout history, it claims. Another story describes a garden with a croaking frog by the Shrine of the Virgin of Guadalupe, with tadpoles swimming under London Bridge. Carson had always wanted to create a major building, just one, and Concrete City was his response.Moving a City, 1998By that decade Carson could no longer care for his invention, and the elements had begun to wear it down. He talked to his family, museum officials and representatives of a local university and he explained his perspective. He figured the city wasn’t going to raise the worth of his house and whoever could move it could have it. "Then he and his family gave the museum the environment it needed.The transfer was carried out in stages. The museum selected Our Lady of Lourdes Cathedral as a test case to see what it would take to move these huge yet delicate items. The sculpture was moved in 1996 and was part of the 1997 exhibition Still Worth Keeping. The remaining structures followed in May 1998, and Carson died later that year at the age of 85.Conservation continued for years after that. Almost all of the sculptures have been stabilised and conserved, with several fully recreated under the leadership of Wisconsin conservator Tony Rajer, the museum reports. That work is based on widely known principles. The National Park Service guidance on historic concrete says, “Maintenance and repair are best accomplished using the principle of minimum intervention and maximum retention of original material, with replacement reserved for badly degraded elements.” It’s a good reminder that concrete, despite seeming permanent, does age like everything else.The necessity of preserving folk art contextsConcrete City is one of a larger group that specialists call art environments, places developed by self-taught creators on their own property. They are tough to save, as they generally rely on the energy of one individual. Still, the preservationist Don Howlett told SPACES Archives that mainstream preservation does not yet acknowledge art spaces as important cultural treasures. He also said that several sites were under threat but more sites have been saved and now have strong organisations behind them. He said the Garden of Eden in Lucas, Kansas, and the Watts Towers were the first preserved in the country.Carson’s work found a different outlet in a state museum eager to take on a backyard full of concrete. Later the museum got a grant from the South Carolina Arts Commission to rehouse the collection with unique shelving and materials so it can keep inspiring for decades to come. Visitors should know that museums rotate artefacts. The State Museum is at 301 Gervais St. in Columbia. It is important to confirm with the museum what is on view before making the journey. The point is straightforward. Carson never got his cathedral but built something more suited to his talent, and a community determined was worth preserving. Concrete City shows that a backyard project may become a museum collection when someone chooses to save it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A North Carolina land trust has saved the first 200 acres around Tuckertown Reservoir after 1,400 donors joined the campaign; another 3,800 privately owned acres remain at risk of sale and development
articles.summary: A conservation campaign in North Carolina has secured the first 200 acres of land around Tuckertown Reservoir, preserving public access to a stretch of
articles.body: A conservation campaign in North Carolina has secured the first 200 acres of land around Tuckertown Reservoir, preserving public access to a stretch of shoreline and forest that has been available to outdoor users for decades. The Three Rivers Land Trust (TRLT), which is leading the Save Tuckertown campaign, announced the completion of the first acquisition in August 2026. According to the organisation, more than 1,400 grassroots donors contributed to the effort, with donations coming from across the US and beyond. The first tract will ultimately be transferred to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission and remain part of the state’s public gamelands.The 200-acre acquisition, however, represents only the first phase of a much larger conservation effort. TRLT says about 3,800 additional acres surrounding Tuckertown Reservoir remain at stake. The land has historically been privately owned by Alcoa but has been enrolled in the North Carolina Gamelands Program, allowing public recreational access. The conservation group is now seeking to acquire additional parcels before they can potentially be sold for development.The first 200 acres are now protectedThe first part of the campaign has now moved from fundraising to a completed land purchase. Three Rivers Land Trust (TRLT) acquired 200 acres around Tuckertown Reservoir and plans to transfer the property to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission. The land will remain available through the state's public gamelands system rather than being closed off for private use.That distinction matters because the property has not historically functioned like an ordinary piece of private land. Although the surrounding acreage has been privately owned, it has been enrolled in the North Carolina Gamelands Program, allowing members of the public to use it for recreation. The campaign attracted support from a surprisingly wide area. TRLT says more than 1,400 grassroots donors contributed, with donations coming from every US state, Guam, Canada and Europe.The fundraising effort also received support from outdoor companies onX and MeatEater, which participated in a matching campaign. The North Carolina Wildlife Habitat Foundation contributed $40,000 toward the priority tract, with the contribution matched by the two companies. For TRLT, the response was a sign that the concern over Tuckertown extends beyond the people who live immediately around the reservoir.Why the shoreline is importantThe land surrounding Tuckertown Reservoir is valuable for reasons that go beyond public access. The forested properties provide habitat for wildlife and help maintain a natural buffer along the reservoir. Keeping large portions of that landscape intact also means the shoreline is less likely to be transformed by development. There is a history behind the current campaign as well. Some land around Tuckertown has already been protected through previous conservation efforts. TRLT points out that the remaining properties were not covered by a 2007 relicensing settlement that resulted in other Tuckertown-area land being conserved. That has left a substantial amount of privately owned property in a different position.The land trust is now working to prevent those remaining parcels from being sold and potentially developed. Its concern is particularly relevant because of the area's proximity to several population centres. TRLT notes that nearly 80% of North Carolina's population lives within 100 miles of the Tuckertown lands. If the properties change hands and are developed, public access to parts of the shoreline could become more limited.Thousands of acres are still at riskThe 200-acre purchase is only the beginning of the Save Tuckertown campaign. TRLT estimates that another 3,800 acres around the reservoir remain at risk of being sold. The organisation is seeking to acquire those properties gradually, depending on funding and opportunities to purchase the land. One of the next major targets is an approximately 800-acre tract. The property includes more than four miles of shoreline and a mature hardwood forest. It also has views of Tuckertown Reservoir from Highway 49. The land trust says properties such as this could be sold at any time. If they are purchased for private development, the character of the shoreline could change considerably, along with the way the public uses the area.TRLT's plan is to step in where possible, purchase the properties and eventually transfer them to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission. The goal is to keep the land within the public gamelands system rather than simply placing it under another form of private conservation ownership.A campaign built around keeping access openThat public-access element is central to the project. Conservation does not always mean that land becomes public. In this case, however, TRLT is deliberately pursuing a route that can keep people on the land. Once properties are acquired, they can remain available for public recreation while arrangements are made for their eventual transfer.The land trust has followed a similar approach elsewhere in North Carolina. According to TRLT, it has helped move more than 8,000 acres into public ownership, including properties around High Rock Lake and along the eastern shoreline of Tuckertown. The first 200 acres at Tuckertown now form another part of that effort.The next phase is much biggerFor the moment, the campaign has a clear achievement to point to: 200 acres have been secured with help from more than 1,400 donors. But the much larger figure is still ahead. With about 3,800 privately owned acres remaining at risk, TRLT's work at Tuckertown is far from finished. The organisation will need to continue raising money and finding opportunities to purchase individual properties. Each successful acquisition could keep another section of shoreline, forest and recreational land from changing hands.For those who already use Tuckertown Reservoir, the first 200 acres offer some certainty. The wider landscape, however, will depend on what happens with the thousands of acres that remain.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Maryland factory built in 1920 once employed thousands making furniture, food and WWII rations; after sitting vacant, it has been restored as a business hub with a new $1 million oyster center
articles.summary: A historic factory in Cambridge, Maryland, built in 1920 has been transformed from a vacant building into a centre for businesses, entrepreneurs, food
articles.body: A historic factory in Cambridge, Maryland, built in 1920 has been transformed from a vacant building into a centre for businesses, entrepreneurs, food production and community programmes. The Packing House, in Dorchester County, was once linked to one of the Eastern Shore’s largest employers and is now being used for new businesses and projects connected to the region’s agricultural and maritime roots.According to Maryland Department of Commerce, the building was originally constructed as the Cambridge Furniture Company. It later became part of the Phillips Packing Company, which supported thousands of residents across Maryland’s Eastern Shore. During World War II, the company produced food products and military rations.After the building was left vacant, it has now been redeveloped by Cross Street Partners in partnership with the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy. The redevelopment has brought new activity to the historic property, which now includes office, retail and event spaces along with areas for environmental companies and non-profit organisations.The Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) has also opened its Cambridge office at the site. The redevelopment is intended to create opportunities for businesses and entrepreneurs while giving a new use to a historic building that had been sitting vacant.From furniture factory to business hubThe Packing House’s history is closely connected to the industries that shaped the Eastern Shore. Its first use was as the Cambridge Furniture Company after it was constructed in 1920. It later became part of the Phillips Packing Company, which grew into one of the region’s largest employers.The packing company produced food products and military rations during World War II. Its operations supported thousands of people in the Eastern Shore community.The building’s latest transformation is focused on keeping it connected to the region’s existing industries. The site now supports businesses and organisations working in areas including aquaculture and environmental technologies.Maria Mougridis, project manager and community planner for DHCD, said the redevelopment of historic properties can help create stronger communities.“Revitalizing historic properties is an important part of building stronger, more sustainable communities across Maryland,” Mougridis said. “Strategic state investment can help transform vacant or overlooked locations into places where businesses can grow, entrepreneurs thrive, and communities come together,” she added.The redevelopment has therefore given the former factory a new role without removing its connection to the area’s history. Along with businesses and organisations, the property is now being used for community programming.$1 million project to focus on oystersA major part of the redevelopment is linked to oysters and environmental work. Last year, DHCD announced a $1 million state revitalisation project at the Packing House.The project is developing a centre focused on oyster processing, biotechnology laboratories, education and ecological stewardship.The work also involves the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science. With support from state funding, the centre established a regional office for Blue Oyster Environmental at the Packing House.Blue Oyster Environmental aims to become the regional leader in re-establishing the Eastern Oyster in the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem. The organisation’s work at the Packing House brings oyster-related research and environmental activities into a building that was once used for furniture production and later food and military-ration manufacturing.Dr Michael Sieracki, director and research professor at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences, said the project is intended to support oyster restoration and environmental stewardship.“Blue Oyster Environmental and UMCES remain incredibly grateful for the state’s continued support. Funding helps us turn our vision for oyster restoration and environmental stewardship into reality,” Sieracki said.He added that the continued expansion of the project would support the future of the Chesapeake Bay. “The continued expansion of this project helps to guarantee the health of our Chesapeake Bay and its future generations,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meta enters new business focused on selling AI tools to enterprise customers, takes on Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI; Mark Zuckerberg says: We believe superintelligence will...
articles.summary: Meta wants companies, not just advertisers, to pay for its AI.
articles.body: Meta wants companies, not just advertisers, to pay for its AI. The Facebook and Instagram parent has launched Meta Enterprise Platform, a new business line that will sell its AI models, agents and coding tools to businesses. The move puts Meta in direct competition with Microsoft and Google for corporate technology budgets.To run it, Mark Zuckerberg has hired Chirantan "CJ" Desai, who until Monday was CEO and President of database company MongoDB. Desai joins as Chief Enterprise Platform Officer and reports directly to Zuckerberg. "We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses," Zuckerberg said, calling the unit "the next major pillar of our business."The exit caught MongoDB off guard. Its shares fell more than 17% on the news, and the board has brought back Dev Ittycheria, who led the company from 2014 to 2025, as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement.Meta Enterprise Platform will sell Muse, Business Agent and Muse Code to companiesThe platform will initially bundle the Muse agent, Meta Business Agent, Muse API and Muse Code for businesses and developers. The timing leans heavily on Muse, the personal AI agent Meta launched on September 8. It can send emails and book travel, and it reached the top of the US App Store and Google Play Store within two weeks. Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates it crossed 3.4 million downloads by September 24.Meta Business Agent, announced in June, already answers customer queries, books appointments and closes sales on WhatsApp, Instagram and Messenger. In August, Meta also released a coding model priced close to lower-cost Chinese open-weight rivals. What Meta has not shared yet is pricing, availability timelines or the admin controls a company would get.Meta's $600 billion AI bill needs revenue beyond adsMeta is spending more than $100 billion on AI infrastructure this year alone, and Zuckerberg expects to spend $600 billion over the next two years. That appetite has made investors nervous. The stock dropped 10% in after-hours trading in July after Meta raised its spending forecast. Muse's success reversed some of that, with shares rising more than 10% last week.Enterprise contracts could offer steadier revenue than consumer subscriptions, which Meta is still trying to sell to Facebook and Instagram users. Desai said that "security and privacy are built into Meta's enterprise products from the outset," a claim businesses will want to test before handing an agent access to company data.Meta's earlier workplace tools shut down, while Microsoft and Google have a head startThis is not Meta's first attempt at selling to companies. Workplace, its internal communication tool launched in 2016, crossed seven million paid subscribers by 2021 but shut down in May 2026. Horizon Workrooms, its VR meeting app, closed in February.The competition is also tougher now. Microsoft redesigned Copilot last week with an autonomous agent that keeps working after employees log off, while Google has years of Workspace and cloud relationships. Coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor already have loyal enterprise users.Desai's resume is Meta's answer to that gap. He spent nearly eight years at ServiceNow, rising to President and COO, and led product and engineering at Cloudflare. Meta has the models and the reach. Whether it can become a company businesses trust for the long haul will depend on the terms it offers next.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 23 US nuclear tests forced Bikini Atoll residents from their homes; decades later, scientists found giant corals thriving underwater
articles.summary: For years, Bikini Atoll has been associated with the destructive legacy of nuclear weapons testing.
articles.body: For years, Bikini Atoll has been associated with the destructive legacy of nuclear weapons testing. Stanford University reported that between 1946 and 1958, the United States detonated 23 nuclear devices across the Marshall Islands atoll, forcing its residents from their homes. The explosions left behind radioactive contamination that prevented permanent resettlement. Yet decades later, the waters around the abandoned atoll presented a very different picture. Marine biologists visiting the lagoon encountered fish, sharks and large colonies of coral. The corals were particularly striking because they could not simply move away from contaminated areas. Some appeared to have begun growing roughly a decade after the nuclear tests, raising questions about how they had managed to persist in an environment exposed to radiation.23 US nuclear tests transformed Bikini Atoll and forced residents into exileThe US nuclear testing programme at Bikini Atoll began in 1946, shortly after the Second World War. Over the following 12 years, 23 nuclear devices were detonated there, radically altering the environment and displacing the island's population. Residents were evacuated with the expectation that they would eventually be able to return. That did not happen. Radioactive contamination remained in the environment, affecting water, vegetation and other resources needed for permanent habitation.By the time marine biologists returned their attention to the atoll decades later, Bikini had become an unusual example of a place where the effects of nuclear testing remained part of the landscape long after the explosions themselves had ended.Fish, sharks and large corals were found thriving around Bikini AtollReportedly, a visit by Stephen Palumbi, director of Stanford University's Hopkins Marine Station and a senior fellow at the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment, revealed a marine environment that was far from lifeless.The lagoon contained fish and sharks, along with large coral colonies. The presence of coral was particularly significant because individual colonies can remain in one location and grow for many years. A fish or shark can move away from an unfavourable environment. Coral cannot.Some estimates placed the beginning of the surviving corals' growth at around 10 years after the nuclear detonations. The colonies had established themselves relatively soon after the testing period and subsequently continued developing in waters affected by radioactive contamination.Earlier coral tests offered a possible clue to Bikini’s surviving reefsPalumbi had already been investigating how coral responds to environmental stress in other parts of the Pacific. His work included experiments involving coral from Samoa, where samples came from locations with different histories of nuclear runoff.The coral exposed to the nuclear-runoff environment behaved differently when tested under warmer-water conditions. In the reported experiments, that sample responded relatively normally, while coral from the comparison site showed a negative response to the increased temperature.The findings did not establish exactly why the Bikini corals were able to persist. Palumbi's work instead pointed towards a possible explanation that required further investigation: populations living under prolonged environmental stress may, over generations, acquire characteristics that help them tolerate those conditions.Bikini’s giant corals offered evidence of long-term survivalThe size and apparent age of the Bikini corals mattered. Their presence could not easily be explained by a short-term return of marine life after the testing programme. Coral grows in place, building its skeleton over time. Large colonies therefore provided evidence that organisms had survived and developed in the lagoon across an extended period. Their persistence also contrasted with the continuing difficulties of human habitation on the atoll, where radioactive contamination remained a problem.The lagoon's fish and sharks added to the picture, but the coral raised the more specific biological question. It was an organism that had remained exposed to the same broad environment rather than simply passing through it.What radiation resistance could mean for biologyAs reported, radiation can damage DNA, with mutations potentially leading to serious biological consequences including cancer. That makes organisms capable of tolerating prolonged exposure of particular interest to researchers.The Bikini observations did not show that coral was immune to radiation or that it had developed a mechanism that could be directly applied to humans. The research was still at the stage of trying to determine what had allowed these populations to survive.If the corals had developed biological mechanisms for dealing with radiation-induced damage, understanding those mechanisms could eventually contribute to research into DNA damage and cellular protection. Any such application would require substantial further research.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Lobster roll war erupts in New England over controversial ingredient in 'die-hard' divide
articles.summary: Maine-style with mayo or Connecticut-style with butter? A Portland lobster roll shop reveals the surprising split among customers ordering each.
articles.body: Ordering a lobster roll "Connecticut-style" in Maine might garner a dirty look — or worse, a side of mayonnaise instead of butter. A recent debate has heated up in Maine over how a proper lobster roll should be served: warm, with butter, or cold, with mayo. Maine-style lobster rolls traditionally consist of cold lobster meat, either tossed in mayo or served with mayo on the side. RED LOBSTER'S 37-YEAR-OLD CEO BETTING ON NOSTALGIA, AI TO FUEL CHAIN'S COMEBACK AFTER BANKRUPTCY A Connecticut-style roll typically includes warm lobster meat, poached in butter or served with warm butter on the side. In both variations, the lobster is piled onto a warm, toasted split-top bun, usually brioche. Despite the discourse over which style of lobster roll reigns supreme, Peter Bissell, co-owner of Highroller Lobster Co. in Portland, Maine, believes there's room for both. SPINY LOBSTER MINI SEASON KICKS OFF IN FLORIDA, DRAWING EAGER DIVERS TO THE WATER "We just want to make people happy with fresh, never frozen, Maine lobster meat, and our specialty mayos was sort of our differentiating factor," he told Fox News Digital. "But we're not dying on any of these hills. It's really good either way." Highroller Lobster Co. is known for its specialty mayos, which come in flavors like roasted red pepper, fresh lime and roasted garlic. Instead of tossing the meat in mayo, the restaurant drizzles the mayo on top of the lobster roll in a zigzag pattern. Those who opt for Maine-style lobster rolls tend to appreciate the tangy mayo combined with "the cool, refreshing interior of the sandwich [and] the crisp, warmed bread on the outside," Bissell mentioned. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER For guests who prefer butter, it's available at Highroller and always has been, Bissell said. It has offered warm butter on cold meat from day one, but warm lobster meat with butter is a relatively recent menu addition. "We added Connecticut-style," Bissell said. "It's a $1 upcharge because the cooks, they poach it in butter for 45 seconds to one minute on the line, so now customers can order fully warmed meat with butter if they choose." Of all the lobster rolls sold this past summer, about 50% were ordered with mayo and 50% were ordered with butter. Of the 50% with butter, 25% were Connecticut-style, according to Bissell. Connecticut-based chef and restaurant owner Robert Marcarelli's approach to lobster rolls is not quite as flexible as Bissell's. His restaurants only sell Connecticut-style lobster, warmed with butter. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Connecticut is very die-hard butter, no mayo. "I will try the mayonnaise ones here and there, but my favorite is just hot lobster with butter," he noted. articles.title: Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage in Channel
articles.summary: Daniel Thomas is remanded in custody after appearing at Portsmouth Crown Court.
articles.body:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel.

Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared via videolink at Portsmouth Crown Court accused of criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at the boat with a knife.

The 37-year-old, whose address was withheld by the court at a previous hearing, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He has been remanded in custody, with a provisional trial date set for 1 March.

The defendant, wearing a grey t-shirt and holding a copy of the Bible, did not enter a plea during the hearing but previously pleaded not guilty to both charges at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Friday.

Thomas is alleged to have used his social media platform to livestream himself from the English Channel at around 16:30 BST on 22 September, broadcasting to a large audience, the court heard.

He is accused of slashing a boat that had been used by migrants, which was adrift in the sea, while a rescue crew member was on board.

He is also alleged to have said "this is what needs to happen" and "this is England, this isn't France any more".

Simon Pentol KC, defending, had proposed a "package of bail conditions" as an alternative to Thomas being remanded in custody and described the allegation against his client as "politically charged and fundamentally flawed".

On his decision to refuse bail, the Judge James Newton-Price KC, said: "I am not concerned with the political issues or motivations in this matter and I put them aside in deciding this matter."

A handful of supporters waited outside the court to hear the outcome of the hearing.

articles.title: 'Indian Americans are as American as anyone': US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi terms debate on immigration racist, xenophobic
articles.summary: US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi strongly condemns recent discussions on Indian immigration, branding them as racist and xenophobic, and emphasizes that Indian Americans are integral to American identity.
articles.body: US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi has pushed back against a debate over Indian immigration in the US, rejecting the idea that Indian Americans should be viewed as an ethnic issue that needs to be addressed.“Indian Americans are not an ‘Indian Question’ to be solved,” the Illinois Democrat wrote in a post on X.Krishnamoorthi said treating an American community as a problem because of its ethnicity was “racist, xenophobic, and fundamentally un-American”.“We are a nation born of ideals, not bloodlines,” he wrote.The congressman added that no race, religion, or ancestry had a greater claim to the US than any other.“Indian Americans are as American as anyone. This country belongs to all of us,” he said.His comments came after Jonathan Keeperman shared a post about a recent episode of the “Rufo & Lomez” podcast, hosted by conservative commentator Christopher Rufo and Keeperman.Released on September 26, the episode is titled “The Indian Question” and focuses on the position of Indian immigrants and Indian Americans in the wider debate over immigration and American identity.The discussion centres on issues including H-1B visas, assimilation, demographic change and the changing role of Indian immigrants in American society. Its published description asks whether the debate surrounding Indian immigration is ultimately about “race, class, or something else entirely”.In his post, Keeperman described Indian immigrants as a relatively small but rapidly growing foreign-born demographic and said their growing presence had made them a visible part of debates over immigration and American identity.Krishnamoorthi's response directly rejected framing Indian Americans as a problem based on their ethnicity, instead arguing that American identity should not be determined by race, religion or ancestry.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Anna Luísa Beserra, a Brazilian scientist whose teenage idea turned dirty water into drinking water using just sunlight; used by 40,000 in 2024 alone
articles.summary: Anna Luisa Beserra is currently known as an environmental entrepreneur. But before she went into business, she was an environmental changemaker.
articles.body: Anna Luisa Beserra is currently known as an environmental entrepreneur. But before she went into business, she was an environmental changemaker. At just 15, she came up with Aqualuz, a system that uses just sunlight to eliminate microorganisms in rainwater without chemicals or complex filters.As a teenager, Beserra was motivated by the lack of clean drinking water for millions of people in Brazil and decided to do something about it. “I knew then that if I created something easy to use and replicate, communities could take control of purifying their own water,” Beserra told UNESCO.The system created by Beserra, called Aqualuz, is affordable, sustainable and designed to last up to 20 years, offering a lasting alternative to temporary filtering solutions. The technology was designed for families relying on rainwater cisterns in semi-arid regions and is already in use in rural Brazil, benefiting more than 10,000 people and reaching 40,000 in 2024 alone.The idea was simple yet precise. Aqualuz is a rainwater treatment system that uses solar radiation to purify collected water safely and affordably by killing microorganisms. The device gave rural households a way to secure clean drinking water without depending on expensive infrastructure or unreliable municipal systems.According to Beserra, scientific research is essential, but it cannot replace firsthand experience with communities. “Meeting families facing water scarcity changed the way I approach solutions. Nothing replaces learning directly from the people you’re trying to help,” he said.Her approach includes training local technicians to lead the installation and monitoring of the systems, making each project a shared effort.Over the years, Beserra, a native of Salvador in Brazil, has earned a degree in biotechnology at the Federal University of Bahia. She has refined the prototype of Aqualuz into a working model and built a social enterprise around it. Today, she is the founder and CEO of Safe Drinking Water for All (SDW), a Brazilian company that designs affordable sanitation and water purification technologies for underserved communities.Beyond Aqualuz, Beserra has developed other solutions such as Aquasalina, which uses sunlight to desalinate water; Aquafilter, a filtration system for communities of up to 100 people; and Aquatorre, designed for schools and areas without water infrastructure.Her goal is to expand these technologies across Latin America, Africa and Asia, providing sustainable access to safe drinking water while strengthening education and local communities’ independence. For her work, Beserra is recognised by the UN, UNESCO and MIT.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: RAF Fairford incident involves 'foreign actor', says Rubio
articles.summary: In a television interview the US secretary of state mentioned Iran, which has denied any involvement.
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor".

In an interview with Fox News on Monday, Rubio said "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally".

He did not provide evidence or further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

A major incident was declared at the weekend after "suspicious vehicles" were seen near the RAF base in Gloucestershire, which has been used by US forces to carry out strikes against Iran.

Dozens of homes were evacuated after the three vehicles were reported to police in the early hours of Sunday morning.

Five men, who are all UK nationals in their 20s, were arrested on suspicion of terror offences, and later released on bail.

On Monday Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), said officers are considering all angles, including that "this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state".

In his comments to Fox News, Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation." He added: "There's a lot more news that'll come out on this in the days to come, but there's only so much I can say right now at this point about it."

The Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what the government calls defensive strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

According to CTP, the five men - aged between 23 and 25 and from London - remain under investigation, and their release is "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others".

Speaking at the White House earlier on Monday, Donald Trump said "I will tell you, I would have said 'Don't let them have bail'. I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham meanwhile chaired a Cobra meeting on Monday and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts".

On Tuesday a heavily guarded police cordon remained in place around the RAF base at Fairford.

Residents of the nearby village of Whelford have been told they can move home. One local told the BBC most people had returned home, but had been told by police to stay inside and not take any photos.

"I haven't gone home as I want to wait until I know more about what the hell happened, as it feels super dodge to me," she said.

Local councillor Tristan Wilkinson said the mood among residents is a mixture of "confusion" and "weariness".

"I don't think there's going to be anything normal about Whelford for quite a considerable amount of time," he told BBC local radio.

In the village of Fairford meanwhile, butcher Andrew Butler said "people are worried, a bit panicky".

"Any suspicious vehicle that people aren't sure about, they think could potentially be a problem," he said.

articles.title: An Essex family set aside its entire farm roughly 30 years ago; after farming resumed in 2014, 50 acres stayed wild, regenerated with oak and scrub, and helped inspire a 200-acre nature-recovery plan
articles.summary: An Essex estate has launched a 200-acre nature-recovery project after seeing how a smaller area of land recovered when it was left untouched for a decade.
articles.body: An Essex estate has launched a 200-acre nature-recovery project after seeing how a smaller area of land recovered when it was left untouched for a decade. The project at Braxted Park Estate covers about 70 hectares across the administrative areas of Colchester City Council, Braintree District Council and Maldon District Council. It builds on a land management decision made decades ago. About 30 years ago, the Clark family decided to set aside their entire farm. After ten years in the Countryside Stewardship scheme, farming resumed in 2014. But the family chose to leave about 50 acres unfarmed. Over the next decade, scrub grew back and self-seeded oak trees matured. The area then attracted rare birds, including turtle doves and nightingales. Duncan Clark DL, owner of Braxted Park Estate and creator of the Braxted Park Habitat Bank, said seeing the natural recovery across those 50 acres persuaded him to expand the work over a much larger area. "The opportunity to increase the acreage of nature recovery to 200 acres of BNG was one Duncan could not turn away from," according to the estate’s official publication detailing the project history. The larger 200-acre project is an off-site Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) habitat bank. Under current UK planning rules, property developers must ensure that new projects deliver at least a 10 per cent increase in local biodiversity. If ecological improvements cannot be made directly on a building site, developers can buy biodiversity units from outside habitat banks to meet the legal requirement.Statutory framework and 30-year binding agreementThe project is in the Northern Thames Basin National Character Area and is designed to support the regional Local Nature Recovery Strategy. The habitat creation and improvement scheme operates under a Section 106 legal agreement. This agreement commits the estate to a 30-year plan for managing and monitoring the habitat. This long-term arrangement gives local planning authorities, developers and ecological consultants legal and practical certainty that the land will be monitored and protected over time. Property consultancy Bidwells is managing the strategy and the commercial sale of the biodiversity units created by the project. James Young, Rural Agency and Natural Capital Sales Manager at Bidwells, is responsible for matching developers' needs with the units available from the estate. He also helps ensure that sales meet legal trading rules and local planning conditions. Further oversight and management support comes from Bidwells' natural capital team. This includes Head of Rural Roland Bull, Natural Capital Partner Lisa Bulmer, and Environmental Consultant Maisie Jimson-Woods.Hands-on stewardship and regional species conservationLocal estate staff and outside conservation experts are managing the work on the ground. Mark Dronfield, BNG Implementation Officer at Braxted Park, grew up on the estate and now oversees planting and habitat management. "I have a personal connection to this land as I grew up here on the estate and I can remember views of newly planted woodland. The same views now are of maturing trees of similar age to me. To come back to Braxted Park and plant new trees myself and steward these new woodlands, hedgerows, grasslands and the wildlife that call this area home is very grounding and fulfilling," said Dronfield. Environmental charities are also providing advice on specific species. Mark Nowers, Turtle Dove Conservation Adviser in Essex for the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), gives advice on creating suitable habitat. Nowers works across a network of about 100 farms, estates and landholdings in Essex. His work supports efforts to create the conditions needed for turtle doves to recover. The species has suffered major population declines across Britain in recent decades. The 70-hectare site combines hedgerows, native grasslands and scrubland with maturing oak woods. Together, these habitats create a continuous ecological corridor across middle Essex. The project allows developers in the Colchester, Braintree, Maldon and Chelmsford planning zones to meet their environmental obligations while creating a permanent area for nature recovery in the Northern Thames Basin.You use AI every day. articles.title: AI 'kill chain': What happens when humans trust bad data at the worst possible moment
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence is the biggest story of our time. It writes code, drafts legal notes, plans wedding menus and reads medical scans.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is the biggest story of our time. It writes code, drafts legal notes, plans wedding menus and reads medical scans. Companies rebrand themselves around it, investors pour billions into it and governments race each other to build it first. Every boardroom, conference and family WhatsApp group seems to have a view on where it is heading.Even my friend Ayush has joined the chorus. This is a man who once needed three phone calls to split a restaurant bill on UPI. Today he lectures me about large language models, prompt engineering and why my job will disappear by 2030.It is easy to laugh at the hype. Most of it is seemingly harmless.But the same technology has moved somewhere far less funny. It now sits inside military command rooms, helping process the information used to decide what gets hit.Two incidents from 2026 show why that matters. In one, a US missile strike destroyed a girls' school in the Iranian city of Minab, killing more than 150 people, including at least 120 children, according to UN findings and reporting on the US investigation. In another, a false intelligence report about a Chinese ship nearly triggered a US military operation after a chatbot misidentified the vessel's cargo.Neither story is as simple as saying that "AI decided to kill".The more unsettling story is quieter: bad information entered a system, moved quickly through it and acquired the authority of a much larger decision-making machine.That is the AI kill chain.But first, what is an AI kill chain?"Kill chain" is old military language. It describes the sequence of steps between finding a potential target and destroying it, taking in everything from surveillance and identification to targeting, authorisation, engagement and assessment.Think of it as a relay race in which the baton is information. Intelligence analysts, imagery specialists, targeteers, lawyers, commanders and operators each handle it at different points. If the baton is wrong at the first handover, everyone can still run perfectly. They just run in the wrong direction.AI changes the speed and scale of that race.Modern military systems can process satellite imagery, drone footage, radar, signals intelligence, open-source information and other data far faster than a team of people could manually. Systems such as Palantir's Maven Smart System can fuse large numbers of data inputs and help analysts identify and assess potential targets.That does not mean a machine simply picks a person and fires a missile. Humans remain involved, and targeting continues to pass through intelligence, legal and command processes. Maven itself does not independently make lethal decisions.But that distinction can be misleading.The important question is not only who presses the button. It is what information reaches the person who presses it, how that information was assembled and how much time they have to challenge it.If the information on the screen is wrong, human involvement at the end of the chain does not magically make the decision sound.Minab: When an old mistake moved at AI speedOn February 28, as the US and Israel began their war with Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajarah Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab.More than 150 people were killed, including at least 120 children, according to the UN and reporting on the US investigation. Bloomberg described it as the deadliest American military targeting error of the 21st century in terms of child casualties.The crucial fact is that the school was not newly identified as a target that morning.The site had once been part of an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval compound, and the US military's intelligence database continued to catalogue it as a military facility even after the site had changed.The real world had moved on.The school had been separated from the neighbouring military compound by new walls and entrances. Satellite imagery showed painted walls, a football pitch and markings for school activities. The school had its own website and appeared on Google Maps. Bloomberg's reconstruction found evidence of these changes going back years.Someone had even noticed.US intelligence analysts had detected changes at the site as early as 2019. But remarks about those changes were entered into a system that was not connected to the primary military intelligence database used for targeting. The information existed. It simply did not reach the people who needed it.That distinction matters because AI did not invent the original mistake.The underlying intelligence was already stale.What AI changed was what happened next.The Minab site, still carrying its old classification, entered the Maven system alongside other potential targets. According to officials involved in the Pentagon's investigation, Maven sat between the initial intelligence inputs and later review stages of the targeting process. Work that could previously take hours was compressed into minutes.Some officials also expected Maven to identify stale information or inconsistencies in the intelligence feeding the system. Investigators have said that expectation contributed to an over-reliance on the technology.The result was not a rogue algorithm. It was something more ordinary and potentially more dangerous: an old error travelling through a faster system.The UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran later said there were reasonable grounds to believe the US was responsible for the Minab strike and concluded that the attack constituted a war crime. Washington has rejected the finding, while the Pentagon's own investigation has focused on failures in the intelligence and targeting process.Who failed: The machine or the people?The answer is both less dramatic and more complicated than either.The Pentagon's investigation has focused on outdated intelligence and failures in the targeting process, but Bloomberg's reporting found that investigators also identified outdated imagery, an over-reliance on AI-assisted targeting and gaps in civilian-harm review.There was also a human-system problem.Civilian-harm mitigation teams across the Pentagon had been sharply reduced. Bloomberg reported that staffing across several such teams had fallen by roughly 90%, while the team at US Central Command had been cut from 10 people to one. No member of that team reviewed the Minab site before the strike.That leaves a revealing picture. The system had more information than ever, but fewer people were available to challenge it.The machine was faster, the humans were fewer and the information underneath both was wrong.That is why the familiar question, "Was it the AI or was it the human?", misses the point. The AI does not need to make the original mistake for it to become part of an AI-enabled failure. If an old piece of information is treated as reliable, incorporated into a sophisticated system and then presented to decision-makers alongside hundreds of other data points, it can acquire a credibility it never deserved.Why use AI at all?It is tempting to conclude that the obvious answer is to take AI out of warfare. The military's argument, however, is much harder to dismiss.Modern warfare produces an overwhelming amount of information. Satellites generate imagery, drones stream video, sensors track movements, intelligence agencies collect signals and analysts monitor open-source information. A modern battlefield can produce more information than humans can reasonably examine in real time.AI can search that ocean of data for patterns that would otherwise take people hours, days or even weeks to find.That is precisely why Maven has spread.In March, the Pentagon formally designated Maven a "program of record", securing its place as a long-term military system and paving the way for broader adoption across the US armed forces. Reuters reported that the system analyses data from satellites, drones, sensors and intelligence sources and assists with targeting while retaining human oversight.The military therefore faces a genuine trade-off. Without AI, humans may miss important information simply because there is too much of it. With AI, humans can process vastly more information, but they also risk accepting a machine-assembled picture without adequately challenging the information beneath it.The problem is not simply that AI can be wrong. Humans have always been wrong. The problem is that AI can make a wrong answer move much faster and look much more complete.Palantir and the machine at the centreMaven is made by Palantir, whose software has become increasingly embedded in US military operations.The system can bring together more than 150 data inputs and help coordinate everything from intelligence and targeting to command and control. Bloomberg reported that, before the Iran war, target-list preparation that had previously taken hours could be condensed into minutes.That speed is the attraction. It is also the danger.A human looking at one outdated database entry might hesitate. A system connecting hundreds of pieces of information can make the same entry appear to be part of a much larger, coherent picture.After the Minab strike, Palantir added capabilities to Maven designed to re-review underlying intelligence, identify information that could disqualify a target and flag inconsistencies that human reviewers might have missed. According to Bloomberg, those tools have already identified anomalies.The fix for an AI blind spot, it seems, is more AI.That may work. But it raises the obvious question: if AI checks the information used by AI, where does the independent challenge come from?The Chinese ship and the chatbotThe second case shows how quickly the chain can become dangerous even without a missile being fired.CNN reported in September that a false intelligence report circulated through the US military during the Iran war. It claimed that a Chinese vessel in the Middle East was carrying components linked to a nuclear weapons programme.The report had been prepared with the help of AI.A special operations analyst had used a chatbot that inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying. The resulting information was turned into what appeared to be a conventional intelligence report and circulated through military channels.The military acted on it.Aircraft were in the air and armed personnel were preparing for a possible boarding. It was only shortly before the planned operation that officials examined the underlying intelligence more closely and discovered that AI had helped generate the report and that the chatbot had misidentified the cargo. The operation was halted.No shots were fired, but the incident demonstrates the same basic problem as Minab.A questionable piece of information entered the system. The system gave it a more authoritative form. Other people trusted that form, and the information travelled much further than the original mistake ever should have.One source told CNN the false report had "almost started a war".The two cases are obviously different. Minab ended in mass civilian deaths; the Chinese ship incident ended with a last-minute correction. Yet they reveal the same vulnerability: a piece of bad information can become increasingly consequential as it moves through a chain of systems and people that assume the previous step was sound.This problem did not begin with AIMilitaries have spent decades discovering that sophisticated systems can still make catastrophic mistakes.In 1999, NATO aircraft struck the Chinese embassy in Belgrade during the Kosovo war. Three Chinese journalists were killed. The strike was attributed to the use of outdated maps.In 1988, the USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Strait of Hormuz, killing all 290 people aboard. The crew misidentified the civilian aircraft during a tense confrontation.In 2003, Patriot missile batteries shot down a British Tornado and a US Navy Hornet over Iraq after automated systems incorrectly classified the aircraft as hostile.These incidents were not caused by generative AI, but they belong to the same family of problems: bad information, complex technology, human pressure and excessive confidence in what the system appears to be saying.The big questionThe debate about military AI is often reduced to one dramatic question: Will a machine eventually pull the trigger by itself?That matters, but it may not be the most immediate question. The more urgent one is simpler: Who checks the information before the trigger becomes the final step?The Minab strike did not require a rogue machine. The underlying mistake existed years before the missile was launched. The Chinese ship incident did not require an autonomous weapon. A chatbot supplied a false piece of information that travelled into a military decision-making system.In both cases, the critical failure came before the final action. A human may still press the button, but by then, the hardest decision may already have been made.The real danger of the AI kill chain is not necessarily a machine deciding who lives and dies. It is one wrong fact moving fast through a system that assumes it is right, with nobody having enough time to stop it.So, in an age of AI-powered warfare, who checks the machine before the machine helps make the decision?You use AI every day. articles.summary: The Facebook founder will clubs €50,000 (£42,000) with donations to be paid over a two-year period.
articles.body:
Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg is taking a step into Irish sports by giving three Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) clubs in County Waterford €150,000 (£129,000).

The clubs are the three closest located to Zuckerberg's newly-purchased Strancally Castle .

Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, plan to give the clubs - Shamrocks GAA, Tallow GAA and Lismore GAA - €50,000 (£43,000) each, with donations to be paid over a two-year period.

A spokesman for Zuckerberg said the couple were "aware of the very significant role that the GAA plays in local communities in Ireland" and as new members of the community, they "wanted to support" the clubs.

It is their first Irish philanthropic donation since they bought the property in August.

BBC News NI spoke to representatives from the clubs to gauge reaction to the donation, with many in their clubs and communities "hugely welcoming" of the gift.

The oldest of the three clubs, Tallow GAA, was founded in 1887.

When Zuckerberg bought Strancally Castle, club treasurer Kieran Geary said he emailed anyone he "could reach out to, in relation to any potential future sponsorship".

Having not heard anything for a couple of weeks, the club secretary, Lyndsey Murphy, then received a phone call from Zuckerberg's team, "just reaching out, discussing" the proposition.

"Initially we were a bit taken a back, was it actually legitimate? And from there things moved fast with Mark's legal team, who were fantastic to deal with," Geary said.

A zoom call was organised with Zuckerberg's team to identify "how Priscilla and Mark might help support us going forward", Geary said.

"His team were so easy going, relaxed, down-to-earth and wanting to support us, wanting to get involved and hopefully visiting the club on the next visit over.

"We also have a few jerseys we are hoping to present to the Zuckerberg/Chan family, due to the donation and how generous they have been," Geary added.

Geary said the aim was to firstly invest the donation in the club's underage teams, before looking to its adult teams and coaching set up.

Then they will invest in the club's community walkway to improve accessibility.

Shamrocks GAA has been operating since 1953, and draws from the combined parishes of Knockanore, Glendine and Kilwatermoy.

The secretary of the club, Tim Lenehan, said at first there was some scepticism about the donation.

"I honestly thought initially it was someone pulling my leg, but we let it evolve and did a bit of checking ourselves and it seemed to be legitimate enough."

The club plans to use the donation to upgrade facilities like changing rooms, as well as develop their underage section.

"We are a very small club, just over 200 members, so obviously fundraising is a hard issue enough because you are usually tapping up the same people all the time for different things, so this is very welcome."

News travels fast in the area, according to Lenehan.

The committee were made aware of the donation on Monday - and everybody in the community "knew by about 8 o'clock this morning," he said.

"The news is very welcome, I think everyone understands the situation with fundraising, it can be difficult you know," he added.

Lismore GAA Club was established in 1897.

Emer Barry, club secretary, said she has known about the donation for about six weeks.

"It's just shock and disbelief. It is hard out figure out at the moment, what's happening and where things are going."

As for a future visit from the couple, Barry said she "doesn't quite know" at the moment if the famous couple will become pitch-side regulars.

The club plans to use the funds to help with projects such as proposed floodlighting, new pitch side fencing and a community walkway.

Regarding Zuckerberg possibly putting on a Lismore jersey, Barry said they were "always open for players, there is no parish rule in Waterford".

articles.title: Angela Rayner announces crackdown on 'cowboy' leasehold property agents
articles.summary: The housing secretary used her Labour conference speech to announce protections for leaseholders facing 'injustice'.
articles.body:
Leaseholders will be given extra protections from "cowboy" property agents and hidden fees, Angela Rayner has announced.

The housing secretary told Labour's annual conference the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap "rip off" administrative fees.

The changes would cover the estimated five million leaseholders in England and Wales who can be forced to pay a landlord for simple changes to their home, despite having bought it.

Rayner told party activists she had heard of leaseholders being charged £250 for permission to own a pet and £400 to change their front door.

She said people in these situations were "powerless against the vested interests that only take, while giving nothing back in return".

The government is already legislating to ban new leasehold flats, described in Labour's 2024 election manifesto as a "feudal" system where people own the right to occupy a property via a lease for a limited number of years from a freeholder, or landlord, who owns the land.

Through the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill , ministers want a commonhold system where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Now, Rayner is taking aim at the web of management companies that operate between leaseholders and their effective landlords.

She said the sector had many decent businesses which were "undermined by far too many cowboys, crooks and con artists".

People excited at buying their own homes are "tricked" into using in-house services, meaning that "with no transparency or accountability, vultures can take advantage", Rayner added.

"We will legislate for an independent regulation to rein these cowboys in," she said, announcing legislation for an independent watchdog of property agents.

This includes estate agents, managing agents and estate managers.

This regulator would be able to set codes of practice, such as standards of conduct and proper complaint handling for those they regulate, and property agents will be required to obtain a licence.

If they fall foul of the required standards, the regulator would have the power to take their licenses away, the government added.

The government said it wanted to bring forward the changes "as soon as possible".

Rayner also said new legislation would create the power for caps on permission and administration fees leaseholders pay to landlords.

These caps would cover freehold estates and privately managed estates where people can face additional fees for making cosmetic changes to their properties and requesting documents like building safety certificates.

A public consultation will be launched to help decide the rate of caps.

It comes in addition to an already-announced £250 cap on yearly ground rents paid by leaseholders in England and Wales, which had stalled during the change of prime minister over the summer.

The government has said it expects the limit on ground rents - an annual fee paid by leaseholders to their freeholder - to come into force in late 2028, but MPs have called for this to be brought forward to late 2027.

Rayner said she was "capping and then scrapping" ground rents, indicating she may try to go further than a cap.

In her speech, Rayner did not mention the government's housing target of building 1.5m homes in England by the next election. She admitted earlier this month there was only a "slim chance" of hitting it .

Last week, ministers announced a new Your First Home policy to help first-time homebuyers in England with a deposit of 2.5%, similar to the Help To Buy scheme introduced under the Conservatives in 2013.

Rayner also said she plans to strengthen council powers to take over empty homes to meet the need for council houses and tackle homelessness.

But this was criticised by the Tories as a "desperate" attempt by Labour to try to hit its housing target.
