articles.title: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home
articles.summary: Two homes belonging to the al-Tubasi family were set on fire and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers.
articles.body:
More than 100 Israeli settlers have carried out attacks in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank, stopping a family escorted by the Israeli military from returning to their homes, which had been seized weeks ago by settlers.

Two houses belonging to the al-Tubasi family in Jalud, south of Nablus, were set on fire in the raid on Monday night and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers. Human rights groups say the events show how Israeli authorities are failing to take effective action against settler violence.

"It was extremely terrifying, beyond words. It's hard to imagine the situation," Mahmoud al-Tubasi told the BBC.

"My feeling now is that I am happy to have escaped death. I genuinely expected they were going to kill us."

Al-Tubasi, 60, his wife Aida, 51, and their 33-year-old son, Wael, had returned to their properties accompanied by Israeli forces after Israel's High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed to go back.

The family was forced to leave this summer after weeks of settler harassment and attacks. Extremist settlers had set up an illegal outpost close to Jalud and besieged three houses, including two belonging to the al-Tubasis' sons who are married with young daughters.

Al-Tubasi said that he was called at about midnight and told that there was coordination with Israel's military for his family to go back to their houses. He received a message from Israeli officials saying that if he wanted to reclaim his property he had to go immediately with the army and Israeli border police.

By torchlight, the family inspected one home. A video shared with the BBC shows that the settlers had already extensively damaged it - smashing holes through doors, tearing out electrical fittings, ripping up tiles, breaking windows and leaving rubbish strewn about. The toilet was smashed and appeared to be full of human waste.

A large number of extremist settlers arrived in Jalud after alerts were posted in WhatsApp groups they use to coordinate action, saying that the Palestinian family they had forced out was returning and should be stopped.

"As soon as we entered the house, which had already been completely destroyed, settlers started throwing stones at us. The army responded by firing tear gas at them, but there were so many settlers, more than 150, that the army could no longer control them," al-Tubasi told the BBC.

The grandfather says that a group of Israeli soldiers protected his family from the settlers who tried to approach them, using pepper spray to force them back. Settlers slashed the tyres of a military van they were put in and then they were transferred to an armoured military vehicle.

As the family was being driven away, the settlers set fire to their car and both of their houses. Video shot from a distance shows smoke billowing from them.

Al-Tubasi says that the Israeli security forces "essentially formed a barrier, took us out safely and got us away from there. But they did not take any action against the settlers themselves."

An Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said that "more than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire, and throwing stones at security forces."

The Israeli military said that three police officers were lightly injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged. It described the Tubasi family as victims of "nationalist crime" adding that "due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed."

The head of the local council in Jalud told reporters that residents had confronted the settlers leading to clashes which even spread to a nearby village, where a Palestinian woman was assaulted by settlers and her house set ablaze.

One month ago, Aida al-Tubasi was attacked by masked Israeli settlers and injured along with American journalists who were interviewing her in Jalud.

The high court decision, which criticised Israeli authorities for failing to crack down on settler violence, ruled that the family should be safely returned home by 20 September - more than a week ago.

The legal ruling was strongly worded describing Israeli settlers' actions as "a completely unacceptable phenomenon that stands in contrast to the basic values and moral principles of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he strongly condemned the attacks on security forces, calling on law enforcement, "to prosecute the rioters to the fullest extent of the law." Israeli police said that they had arrested three people suspected of being involved in the attacks.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly last week, Netanyahu dismissed international concerns about settler violence. He accused the media of ignoring attacks on Jewish Israelis and covering "a handful of juvenile delinquents , about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires."

According to the Israeli human rights group, Yesh Din, fewer than three per cent of police investigations into settler violence over the last two decades have led to a conviction.

Ziv Stahl, its executive director, said the lack of effective law enforcement was because, "the violence is part of a systematic government policy aimed at pushing Palestinians out of the area and expanding Israeli control over land in the West Bank".

Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank claiming biblical and legal rights to the land. Some ministers have said they aim to "bury the idea" that an independent Palestinian state could be set up in the territory along with East Jerusalem and Gaza. Settlements and outposts are illegal under international law.

Levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high this year, according to the United Nations, which says that since 2023, more than 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks and access restrictions in the occupied West Bank.

According to OCHA, at least 82 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank this year and four Israelis have been killed - members of the security forces and civilians. At least 23 Palestinians were killed in the context of settler attacks.

articles.body: The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has released footage of an attack by its newly formed female unit on a Pakistani military convoy in Turbat, claiming that nine security personnel were killed in the operation.The video, released through the group’s media cell Aashoob, shows fighters of the Karima Armed Assault Division (KAAD) firing at a three-vehicle Quick Response Force (QRF) convoy on the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) highway on September 22.The footage includes a female commander briefing fighters before the operation, along with training clips. It also shows the fighters opening fire on the convoy from close range. The group claimed that several military vehicles were severely damaged and that several personnel were injured. These claims could not be independently verified.BLF spokesperson Major Gwahram Baloch said the group’s Qurban unit supported the operation and helped its fighters resist an attempt by Pakistani forces to encircle them, while covering their withdrawal. He said Qurban unit fighter Chakar Murad, alias Dileep Jan, was killed during the attack.The video also shows KAAD members conducting snap checks of vehicles in the Mangchar area of Kalat. articles.title: Man released on bail after 41 years on death row in Utah
articles.summary: New DNA analysis did not match Douglas Stewart Carter, now 71, who was convicted of killing a woman but always maintained his innocence.
articles.body:
A man who spent 41 years on death row in the US after being convicted of killing a woman has been released on bail after prosecutors said newly analysed DNA evidence did not link him to the crime.

Douglas Stewart Carter, who is now 71, was jailed for the killing of Eva Olesen in Utah in 1985.

He was sentenced to death but always maintained his innocence, stating that a signed confession was coerced.

The state Supreme Court ordered a new trial last year, citing misconduct by investigators, and a judge bailed Carter on Monday despite objections from the victim's family. He is required to wear a GPS monitor while on bail.

Olesen, the aunt of a local police chief, was stabbed multiple times and then shot in the back of her head at her home in Provo, Utah, in February 1985.

Carter, who is originally from Chicago, had been living with his mother in Utah at the time of the killing. Court documents show that police suspected him of killing Olesen during a robbery.

Believing he was a suspect in an unrelated case, Carter fled Utah but was eventually found in Nashville, Tennessee. He then signed a confession while under interrogation which he later said was coerced.

Despite there being no physical evidence linking Carter to the crime scene, he was convicted by a jury based on the confession and the testimony of two witnesses who said he had bragged about the murder.

But the witnesses later said in 2011 that they were told to lie in court, given cash and gifts by police and were threatened with deportation if they did not testify against Carter.

After more than a decade, the Utah Supreme Court last year ordered a new trial.

Lawyers representing Carter, who is black, said witnesses had seen a white man fleeing the scene of the murder and that an investigator had suppressed evidence pointing to the victim's husband, Orla Olesen.

They allege that prosecutors were close to filing charges against him, but a police officer asked them not to so he could continue investigating.

Olesen's husband, who died in 2009, told police he had found his wife dead in their home.

The victim's stab wounds were said to have been caused by a knife from their kitchen, which was discovered near her body. The gun was not found at the scene.

Then this month, prosecutors said that results of a DNA analysis excluded Carter as a possible match to blood found on a doorknob and genetic material recovered from the handle of the knife.

Carter's release comes against the wishes of Olesen's family.

Theresa Olesen, a daughter-in-law of Eva Olesen, said during Monday's bond hearing that her family had "serious concerns" about Carter's release. She said he should remain in jail while awaiting a new trial.

"By golly we were hoping for a concrete match," Olesen said of the DNA analysis. "It doesn't mean he wasn't there."

But Carter's defence attorney, Neal Hamilton, called for the case to be dismissed.

"If the state of Utah had their way, he would have been executed 15, 20 years ago before we discovered the misconduct," he told Associated Press.

articles.title: In 1979, Ted Turner bought a 4,680-acre South Carolina barrier island to prevent development; 38 years later he sold it to the state for $4.9 million, about one-third of its appraised value, and it became state parkland
articles.summary: American media mogul Ted Turner has completed the sale of St Phillips Island, a pristine 4,680-acre barrier island off the coast of South Carolina, to the
articles.body: American media mogul Ted Turner has completed the sale of St Phillips Island, a pristine 4,680-acre barrier island off the coast of South Carolina, to the state government for a small part of its market value. The deal transfers ownership of the untouched coastal island to the South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism for $4.9 million. The purchase price is about one-third of the property’s appraised market value of $14.9 million. This means the remaining value represents a large charitable contribution to the public. The land is near Beaufort and just south of Saint Helena Island. It will now become part of the state park system. Under the agreement, the state plans to protect its sensitive ecosystems while allowing limited public access, educational programmes and eco-tourism opportunities.Preserving a pristine islandTurner bought St Phillips Island in 1979 to protect it from commercial development. At the time, coastal areas across the American South were seeing rapid residential construction. For nearly four decades, the media mogul and conservationist used the island as a private family retreat. He kept most of the land completely undeveloped. The island has dense maritime forests, salt marshes, tidal creeks and ancient sand dunes. It is home to many wildlife species, including loggerhead sea turtles, fox squirrels, painted buntings and wood storks. According to official property records and statements from the South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism, Turner placed the island under a conservation easement held by the Nature Conservancy in 1983. The legal agreement permanently limits future commercial development. It ensures that the natural landscape will remain protected regardless of who owns the property.Facilities and access plansThe main human structure on the island is a single-storey, five-bedroom home that Turner built for his family. The property also has a manager's residence, a fishing pier and a small network of dirt trails. The state agency plans to keep these existing structures instead of building new ones. The South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism said the main Turner house will be available for private rentals and retreat bookings. The money raised will help pay for the island’s management and upkeep. Public access will be tightly controlled to prevent damage to the environment. The state plans to run guided boat tours from nearby Hunting Island State Park. Small groups of visitors will be able to explore St Phillips Island using hiking trails and boardwalks.Terms of the state acquisitionTurner and state officials negotiated for several months before completing the final transfer. Funding for the $4.9 million purchase came from a mix of state conservation funds, public grants and park revenue reserves. In a press statement released by the South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism, agency officials confirmed that the deed contains strict conditions. These conditions ensure the island remains dedicated to public enjoyment and natural preservation forever. Duane Parrish, director of the South Carolina Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism, praised the agreement. He said the acquisition adds a rare gem to the state’s public land network. Parrish noted that obtaining an intact barrier island of this size would normally be financially impossible for a state agency without major philanthropic support from the landowner. Turner, who founded CNN and TBS, has long been one of North America’s largest private landowners. He owns hundreds of thousands of acres across several states that are dedicated to conservation and bison restoration. Representatives for Turner said he was pleased that the island would remain untouched and available to future generations under public management. The park service plans to begin limited public ferry services and guided day trips after safety inspections and basic infrastructure checks are completed.You use AI every day. articles.title: Windsor Castle visit as amputee, 9, meets the Princess of Wales
articles.summary: Albie-Junior Thomas had his foot removed as a child but has since scaled the UK's highest mountains.
articles.body:
A nine-year-old amputee who completed the Three Peaks challenge alongside his dad has met Catherine, Princess of Wales to celebrate his success.

Albie-Junior Thomas, from Holywell, Flintshire, was invited for a tea party at Windsor Castle after his father sent a letter describing how he had climbed the highest mountains in Wales, Scotland and England .

Dad Daniel said he thought the message would resonate with the princess, after she completed her own Three Peaks challenge earlier this year, in aid of the hospital where she was treated for cancer.

In a post on X, the princess said it was a "pleasure" to hear the stories of "resilience, determination and hope" shared by each person she met.

The youngster from Holywell, Flintshire, was born without a fibula in his left leg and his foot was removed at 15 months.

Despite this, at four he became the youngest amputee to scale Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, Wales' highest peak.

Albie-Junior and his father have since embarked on several climbing challenges together raising thousands for their local football club in the process.

In August, he finished the Three Peaks Challenge in 22 hours and 30 minutes alongside his dad, powered by ham and cheese sandwiches, sour sweets and four months' training.

This included conquering Ben Nevis in Scotland and Scafell Pike in England as well as Yr Wyddfa.

Daniel described the moment they received a phone call inviting them to Windsor Castle as "unbelievable".

Once they arrived, Daniel said he stayed in the background, letting Albie-Junior enjoy the experience as "it was his thing".

"For him it was just like a chat to a lady, you know, just the innocence of it," he said.

He said the conversation stood out to him because of how "pleasant" it was and said Catherine made him like they were "both equals".

In a post on X, the princess said: "Listening to their experiences of the challenge and their reasons for taking it on was a powerful reminder that recovery is rarely a journey we make alone, and of the importance of the people who walk alongside us along the way."

Despite getting millions of view on their social media channels, Daniel said his son is still as humble as ever, and he reminds him all he has done is "walk up a few mountains".

"To him, it's he's just doing what boys should do. Getting out and having fun," added Daniel.

"It's not like it's for the fame or nothing like that."

Talking about his sons experiences with the princess, he said: "As long as you're nice with someone else and they're nice back, you know that's the way it should be."

Daniel said they are planning to tackle Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, and are gathering up ten others to climb it with them in August next year.

He added: "When there's a challenge set you want to get it done, but it's not just about that because you have to acclimatise and get the safety right."

Daniel said he intends to contact Guinness World Records as Albie-Junior could become the youngest amputee to climb the mountain.

"Yeah I'm determined to get him in it," he added.

articles.title: Meet Zhang Zhanshuo: The 19-year-old who won seven golds at the Asian Games; from a kid who ‘couldn’t swim’ to a Chinese swimming star
articles.summary: At six, Zhang Zhanshuo was the youngest swimmer in a local competition and had barely begun learning the sport.
articles.body: At six, Zhang Zhanshuo was the youngest swimmer in a local competition and had barely begun learning the sport. At 19, he left the Asian Games 2026 with seven gold medals and a place in the record books. The Chinese swimmer became the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single Asian Games when he won the men's 400m freestyle at the Aichi-Nagoya Games on September 25. His seven golds also equalled the Asian Games record for the most individual gold medals won at a single edition, a mark that had stood for 44 years. He competed in eight events and won seven of them. His gold medals came in the men's 200m, 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, along with three relay titles. His 200m freestyle victory also produced an Asian record, while his 400m and 800m wins came in Games-record times. But Zhang's relationship with swimming began for a much simpler reason.‘A seaside kid’ who had to learn to swimZhang was born in Qingdao in May 2007. His mother had been a middle-distance runner for the Shandong provincial team, while his father had also competed in athletics when he was younger, according to reports from Chinese media Qingdao. His father, Zhang Xunshan, has recalled that the original idea was not to turn his son into a professional swimmer. They lived in a coastal city, and he felt that a child growing up by the sea should at least know how to swim.Zhang started learning when he was around five and a half to six years old. As reported by Qingdao News, he trained for about half a year before entering the 2013 Qingdao primary and secondary school swimming competition. He was below the minimum age for the competition, but that did not stop him from taking part. The result surprised everyone. The six-year-old Zhang, the youngest competitor at the event, won six gold and two silver medals. At that stage, there was little indication that the boy would eventually become one of China's leading swimmers.A year later, Zhang was selected by Qingdao swimming coach Liu Ziqian and began systematic training with the city team. Liu later recalled that Zhang was the youngest swimmer in the group, training alongside athletes who were three or four years older.His family came from sportZhang's parents understood the demands of competitive sport themselves. His mother had competed in middle-distance running for the Shandong provincial team, while his father had been involved in athletics. That background also helped his first coach recognise his physical potential. “When I took over, Zhang Zhanshuo was just over seven years old,” Liu told Qingdao Daily. “This child had talent from a young age because his mother had been a middle-distance runner for the Shandong team, and his father had also been an athlete when he was young.”Zhang's rise was gradual after that. He began making a name for himself at provincial competitions before breaking through on the national stage as a teenager.By 16, he had won two gold medals at the 2023 Chinese National Swimming Championships. In 2024, he was part of China's world-championship-winning 4x200m freestyle relay team.The swimmer who keeps coming from behindOne of Zhang's defining moments came during the men's 4x200m freestyle relay at the 2026 Asian Games. China was behind Japan going into the final leg. Zhang took over the anchor position and gradually closed the gap before overtaking Japan in the final stretch. His split was 1:42.92, and China finished in 7:00.17, breaking the Asian record. After the race, Zhang was asked about the dramatic comeback. His answer was short: “Normal, normal.” His teammate Pan Zhanle had a very different way of describing what had just happened. Pan, who had previously been Zhang's childhood hero and was his teammate in the relay, called him a “miracle child” after the race.Seven golds and a new recordZhang's biggest moment came four days later. On September 25, he won the men's 400m freestyle, setting a Games record and securing his seventh gold medal of the competition. After touching the wall, Zhang sat on the lane line and counted his medals on his fingers. “1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7!” “Just after I got out of the water, I counted my gold medals from one to seven. I wanted to express that I had won seven gold medals,” he told the media.His seven golds equalled the record for the most individual gold medals won at a single Asian Games. The previous record had belonged to North Korean shooter So Gil-san, who won seven golds at the 1982 New Delhi Games. Zhang also became the Chinese athlete with the most gold medals at a single Asian Games.He still gave himself '85 out of 100'Despite the seven gold medals, Zhang did not describe his Asian Games campaign as perfect. As reported by Xinhua, he gave himself a score of 85 out of 100 and said he still had technical areas to improve, particularly his turns. Zhang said after the Games: “One step short of perfect.” He also made it clear that the seven medals were not where he wanted the story to end. “The Asian Games is not the goal. I'm still aiming for the Olympics and competing with the best,” Zhang said, according to the South China Morning Post.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Forgotten coffee brands Americans grew up with — and what happened to them
articles.summary: Starbucks and Dunkin' Donuts reshaped coffee culture, but brands like Gold Shield and Savarin still stir powerful nostalgia this National Coffee Day.
articles.body: Long before Starbucks became shorthand for coffee culture, Americans were opening cans of coffee from brands like Gold Shield, Savarin and Schilling. This National Coffee Day, many of those once-familiar names exist mostly in memory. But that may be exactly why they still resonate. "I think there's a lot of nostalgia and romance around coffee because I do think it's such an important part of daily life," said Wendy Pojmann, a professor of history at Siena University who has studied coffee culture and wrote "Espresso: The Art and Soul of Italy." 6 ICONIC AMERICAN RESTAURANTS STILL SERVING UP NOSTALGIA AND CLASSIC FLAVORS For people who grew up with those brands, Pojmann said the connection often goes beyond what was in the cup. "So, I do think that, especially if you grew up and you smelled the coffee in the kitchen and maybe your mom and dad or your grandparents were preparing a certain kind of coffee, those memories are important, and we associate memory with smell," she told Fox News Digital. Coffee culture looked different then, too. Convenience helped define the American coffee routine, from instant coffee to the automatic drip machines that became fixtures in American kitchens. "Americans, again, were interested in ease, efficiency, things being relatively quick," Pojmann said, describing a routine that might include grabbing a big can of Folgers from the grocery store and brewing it at home. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Folgers and Maxwell House endured, but plenty of other familiar names did not. Smaller regional and local coffee brands were often acquired by larger companies, Pojmann said, part of a cycle of consolidation that has played out repeatedly in the coffee business. Gold Shield, a once-popular West Coast brand, and Savarin, a longtime East Coast favorite, were among the coffee labels that eventually disappeared after changing hands. Their fate reflected a broader consolidation in the coffee business, as larger companies acquired smaller regional and local brands, Pojmann said. Then came another shift. Chains such as Starbucks and Dunkin' helped reshape American coffee culture, followed by the rise of specialty coffee and a new generation of small roasters and boutique brands. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ More recently, specialty coffee has created another generation of small roasters and boutique brands. Pojmann said today's coffee market includes everything from huge national brands to tiny small-batch roasters. Still, a coffee brand doesn't necessarily disappear when its cans leave supermarket shelves. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Pojmann said she sometimes spots tins from bygone brands in vintage and antique stores, where an old label can unexpectedly reconnect someone with the past. "Maybe you hadn't thought of it in years and then you see that label on the can and you think, 'Oh yeah, I remembered my grandfather used to make that coffee for us,'" Pojmann said. But the smell of a pot brewing can still bring back memories of the people who once poured it.

articles.title: In 2021, billionaire Orlando Bravo paid $39.25 million for Phil Collins’s 1929 Miami Beach mansion; months later, he won approval to demolish it for a flood-resilient home with tropical gardens
articles.summary: Private equity billionaire Orlando Bravo has received approval to tear down a historic Miami Beach estate once owned by English musician Phil Collins.
articles.body: Private equity billionaire Orlando Bravo has received approval to tear down a historic Miami Beach estate once owned by English musician Phil Collins. The move clears the way for a flood-resistant luxury mansion surrounded by tropical gardens. Bravo, co-founder and managing partner of Thoma Bravo, bought the Mediterranean Revival home at 5800 North Bay Road for $39.25 million (£28.6 million) in January 2021. According to property records cited by the Miami Herald, the purchase was made through an entity called 5800 NBR LLC. Only months after completing the deal, the private equity executive asked local authorities for permission to demolish the 1920s home and build a new single-family compound designed to meet modern environmental standards. The Miami Beach Design Review Board gave final approval for the demolition and new design later that year, after receiving detailed plans from Bravo’s architectural team. The decision ended a long-running debate over whether the estate should be preserved. The property sits on a 1.2-acre waterfront lot along Biscayne Bay.Historic architecture facing climate realityBuilt in 1929, the original two-storey home had more than 10,000 square feet of living space. It included classic Mediterranean Revival features such as barrel-tile roofs, arched doorways, a courtyard layout and detailed ironwork. Before Bravo bought the estate, it attracted international attention because of its famous owners. Phil Collins, the former Genesis frontman and solo artist, bought the home in 2015 for $33 million. Collins lived there until a high-profile legal dispute with his ex-wife, Orianne Cevey, resulted in the property being put on the market in late 2020. Despite its architectural history and links to well-known owners, including Jennifer Lopez, who lived there in the early 2000s, the building was not given protected historic landmark status by the city of Miami Beach. Local rules allow owners of properties without such a designation to seek demolition, as long as replacement projects follow zoning rules and design review standards. The Miami Herald reported that architectural advisers working for Bravo pointed to structural problems and concerns about rising sea levels as key reasons for replacing the original building.Designing for future flood risksBravo’s replacement plans focus strongly on sustainability, flood protection and adapting to environmental changes. Coastal South Florida faces growing risks from rising sea levels, high-tide flooding and powerful tropical storms. As a result, wealthy property owners across Miami-Dade County are rebuilding homes at higher levels than older buildings. Documents submitted to the Miami Beach Design Review Board describe a modern residence made up of several connected sections and raised well above current city requirements. The new design includes elevated foundations, reinforced seawalls and built-in drainage systems. These features are intended to protect the home from severe weather and future sea-level rise. Architect Kobi Karp, whose firm designed the replacement estate, stressed the need for modern engineering on waterfront properties. In presentations to the design board reported by the Miami Herald, Karp said the new design places living areas on raised platforms. This would allow floodwater to move underneath the home during extreme flooding without damaging the main structure. The design also gives priority to native plants and tropical gardens. Landscape plans filed with the city show large green areas with drought-resistant plants, native shade trees and surfaces that allow water to soak into the ground and reduce stormwater runoff.Preservation debates in South FloridaThe decision to demolish the former Collins estate highlighted a wider debate in South Florida real estate between historic preservation and the need to adapt to climate risks. Preservation advocates in Miami Beach have often raised concerns about the loss of early 20th-century architecture along North Bay Road and Star Island. These areas have attracted wealthy buyers who often purchase older homes mainly for the value of the land. The Daniel Heller Historic Preservation Fund and local residents raised questions at public hearings about whether parts of the 1929 home could be restored or included in the new design. However, representatives for the owner submitted engineering reports saying that bringing the existing building up to current South Florida Building Code storm standards would be technically impractical and financially unviable. Under Miami Beach rules, the Design Review Board decides whether proposed replacement homes fit the architectural character of the neighborhood, even when the existing building is being demolished. The board ultimately voted in favour of Bravo’s project, citing the quality of the proposed design and its compliance with modern environmental codes.A changing North Bay Road landscapeBravo’s project is part of a wider trend along North Bay Road, one of Miami Beach’s most prestigious residential areas. Over the past decade, wealthy individuals and finance executives moving to South Florida from New York and California have increasingly bought older luxury estates with plans to replace them with modern homes. Forbes has recognized Bravo as Wall Street’s first Puerto Rican-born billionaire. He moved to South Florida around the time of the purchase as his firm expanded its operations in Miami. Construction at the North Bay Road property began after final building permits were issued. The project is planned to include a main residence, guest house, dock facility and extensive outdoor amenities arranged around the redesigned tropical gardens.You use AI every day. articles.title: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.summary: The prime minister says he wants other parties to take part in a national commission on electoral reform.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.

In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.

He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".

He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".

Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.

Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.

Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.

In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less 30% of the vote or less."

He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."

Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.

Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.

However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.

Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging after Burnham's speech that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.

Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.

At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.

Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.

Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system .

articles.title: Dist collectors told to inspect mid-day meals in schools across Raj
articles.summary: Rajasthan orders district collectors to inspect mid-day meals in 20% of govt schools, Sanskrit schools and madrassas after milk supply lapses and illness reports.
articles.body: Jaipur: The state govt has instructed all district collectors to conduct intensive inspections of mid-day meals being served in govt schools across the state Tuesday and Wednesday.As part of the exercise, each district will cover 20% of schools, including those that have not been inspected in the last two years. The inspection reports have to be submitted by Wednesday evening.The exercise is being conducted following reports of milk not being supplied properly in schools and children falling ill after consuming mid-day meals.“District collectors have been asked to inspect mid-day meals at a minimum of 20 schools selected randomly from district and block headquarters. Collectors may deploy officials from departments other than education to ensure impartial inspections,” an official from the midday meal department said.The inspection will cover all categories of schools, including govt schools, Sanskrit schools and madrassas.Officials said the inspection is conducted bi-annually, in Feb and Sept, to check the quality of food being served, storage of grains and raw material in schools and cleanliness of areas where food is prepared, among other factors.“Based on the inspection, action will be taken if quality is found not up to the mark in any particular district. Schools have been instructed to ensure that midday meal service does not stop, despite lack of funds or delayed release of funds to cook cum helper.
